hero.title: Couples Living Together Test | Are You Ready to Move In?
hero.intro1: You already sleep at each other's place 5 nights a week. You have a toothbrush at his place, he has a drawer at yours. At this point, the question isn't "do we love each other enough to live together" but rather: can we share 600 square feet without killing each other?
hero.intro2: Because living together isn't just extending the weekends. It's discovering that the other person leaves their socks lying around. That their definition of "clean" isn't the same as yours. That silence for two isn't the same as silence alone. And that those cute little habits from the first months can become really annoying after six.

seo.s1Title: Moving in together: the real test for your relationship
seo.s1p1: Everyone tells you it's "the next step." After a few months of dating, the question comes up. "What if we got a place together?" Sounds simple. It isn't.
seo.s1p2: Living together means going from the "best version of yourself" to the "full version." It's a real-life crash test for your relationship. Post-move-in breakups almost never come from the big issues. They come from the daily micro-frictions that pile up.
seo.s1p3: The toothpaste tube. The bedroom temperature. The volume of the music in the morning. Ridiculous? Yes. But after 6 months, a poorly squeezed toothpaste tube can become the symbol of everything you never said.
seo.s2Title: The 6 topics nobody brings up (that ruin everything)
seo.s2r1Text: Not "we'll split things." Specifically. Who pays for what? Joint account or not? 50/50 or proportional to income? Couples who lay out the numbers before signing the lease avoid 80% of money-related arguments.
seo.s2r2Text: It's the division of chores that creates the most resentment in cohabiting couples. At first, one person does more because "it doesn't bother them." Then it becomes expected. Then a frustration. Then a reproach.
seo.s2r3Text: Loving someone and needing alone time aren't contradictory. But when you share 500 square feet, "I need some space" can sound like rejection. Couples who know each other well handle this naturally.
seo.s2r4Text: One gets up at 6 AM to go running. The other works until midnight. These schedule gaps, when you're living together 7 days a week, become a real issue.
seo.s2r5Text: Your apartment is also the other person's home. Home is a refuge. When that refuge is invaded without your consent, it breeds resentment. Set the rules together.
seo.s2r6Title: The "what if it doesn't work out?" question
seo.s2r6Text: Nobody wants to think about it. Who keeps the apartment if you break up? Whose name is on the lease? Talking about this doesn't jinx anything. It protects both of you.
seo.s3Title: How long should you date before moving in together?
seo.s3p1: 6 months. 1 year. 2 years. Everyone has an opinion. The reality is that there's no magic number.
seo.s3p2: What matters is what you've experienced together, not the number of months on the clock. The real criterion: have you already been through a serious conflict? Have you seen each other at your worst?
seo.s3p3: A couple in love is great. A couple in love that knows what daily life together actually looks like is even better.
seo.s4Title: Moving in for the right reasons (and not the wrong ones)
seo.s4p1: The right reasons: you want to build a daily life together, you've tested it and it works.
seo.s4p3: "It'll be cheaper for two." Moving in together to split the rent is a roommate plan, not a couple plan.
seo.s4p4: "It's been 2 years, it's time." The social calendar has nothing to do with your emotional calendar.
seo.s4p5: "We'll see how it goes." Couples who know how to solve their problems are the ones who last under the same roof.
seo.s5Title: The first 3 months: what nobody tells you
seo.s5p1: The first 3 months of cohabitation are the adjustment period.
seo.s5p2: Month 1 is the excitement. Everything is new.
seo.s5p3: Month 2, habits settle in. And the first frictions along with them.
seo.s5p4: Month 3 is the moment of truth. The excitement has worn off, reality is here.
seo.s5p5: Keep some "me time" even when you're living together. That's what helps you keep things light in your relationship.
seo.s6Title: Practical checklist before moving in together
seo.s6p1: The concrete points to sort out before you unpack your boxes in the same place:
seo.s6p2: The budget. Make a spreadsheet. Rent, utilities, groceries, going out, savings.
seo.s6p3: The lease. Under whose name? Both names on the lease = both responsible for the rent.
seo.s6p4: The furniture. Who brings what? What do you buy together?
seo.s6p5: The ground rules. Just a verbal agreement on the things that matter: cleanliness, guests, noise, personal space.
seo.faqTitle: Frequently asked questions about living together

faq.q: Is it normal to feel stressed about moving in together?
faq.a: Yes. It's actually a good sign. The "will we make it work?" kind of stress is healthy.

faq.q: Should you do a trial run before signing a lease?
faq.a: It's not mandatory, but it's smart. Spend 3-4 consecutive weeks at one person's place in full daily-life mode.

faq.q: How do you handle income differences when living together?
faq.a: A strict 50/50 split isn't the only option. Many couples opt for a proportional split based on income.

faq.q: Will moving in together kill the passion?
faq.a: Not if you're intentional about it. Couples who maintain rituals and moments of intimate connection are the ones who thrive.

faq.q: What if one person is ready and the other isn't?
faq.a: Don't force it. Moving in together is a two-person decision or it's no decision at all. If you're struggling to communicate about it, it might be a sign that certain patterns in your relationship are surfacing.

faq.q: Is it better to rent a new place together or move into one person's apartment?
faq.a: Ideally, a fresh space for both of you. Moving into "the other person's place" creates an imbalance.
